B: Hiya! Can you hear me?
A: Yeah, hi, I can hear you. I'm Gemma, Maidstone.
B: Hannah, Norwich. Last one, isn't it? I'm starting to get the hang of these.
A: I know, I'm a bit talked out, to be honest. It's been a long week. So what do you do?
B: I'm a senior midday supervisor at a primary school, so I run the lunchtime team, and I do breakfast club in the mornings. And I'm doing an Open University degree part-time, in the evenings.
A: Oh right. What's the degree in?
B: Arts and Humanities. I'm in my third year. I started a History of Art degree at nineteen and left after the first year because I was skint, so this is sort of me finishing what I started.
A: Funny, I did the same, sort of. I started business at Canterbury Christ Church and left after a year to go and work. Never went back.
B: Oh, really? Do you ever think about it?
A: Erm, not really. I did my Propertymark qualification while I was working, and I'm a branch manager now, so it worked out. Some of my friends went off to uni and, you know, good for them. I've got a team of five, I'm doing alright.
B: No, that's brilliant. I think you learn more working half the time anyway.
A: You do. Is it a lot, though, with a kid? I'm guessing you've got one, from the drawing in your photo.
B: Yeah, Isla, she's nine. She's horse-mad, hence the horse. It's just me and her, so it's busy, but my mum helps with pick-ups.
A: Mine's twelve, Maisie, Year 8. It's a whole different world, secondary.
B: Is she enjoying it?
A: Erm, sort of. It's the friendship stuff, isn't it? Group chats, who's been left out of what. She says she's fine but I'm not sure she is. It keeps me up, honestly.
B: Oh, that's hard. I see it at lunchtimes, even in primary, the little groups forming. The ones who seem fine are sometimes the ones who aren't saying anything. Sorry, I'm not trying to be all teacher about it.
A: No, it's alright. What do you do, then, when one of them's left out?
B: Mostly I just give them a job. Like, can you help me with the hoops, and then another kid wanders over, and suddenly they're playing. It sounds daft but it works. Clubs are a good shout at secondary, something where she's not relying on the same group.
A: Yeah. She did mention drama club. I might push that.
B: Worth a go. And twelve's rough, honestly, I was awful at twelve.
A: Ha, so was I. So what do you do to unwind, when you're not doing essays?
B: Sketching, mostly. Old buildings, market stalls. And I'm in a book group at the library. Very rock and roll.
A: Love Island and a glass of rosé, me. That's my culture.
B: Ha! No judgement. I've watched a bit of it at my mum's.
A: It's a load of rubbish. But I'll still watch every episode. Do you get away much, holidays?
B: Caravan in Wells-next-the-Sea, usually. I'm saving for Florence, very slowly, in a jar.
A: Florence would be nice. I'm all-inclusive, though, I need a pool and someone bringing me a cocktail, otherwise it's not a holiday.
B: Honestly, someone bringing me a cocktail sounds amazing right now. I was absolutely shattered after chips Friday, the queue was...
